title: The Fisherman Who Invented Tsunami Warnings
event_summary: When village headman Goryo Hamaguchi felt an earthquake and noticed the sea receding unnaturally, he set fire to his own harvested rice sheaves on the hillside above the village of Hiro. The blazing stacks drew confused villagers uphill to fight the fire, inadvertently saving their lives moments before a massive tsunami from the Ansei-Nankai earthquake obliterated the coastal settlement. He then spent his personal fortune over the next four years building a massive seawall and replanting coastal forests, creating one of the world's first engineered tsunami defense systems.
why_forgotten: Hamaguchi's story was celebrated locally and briefly taught in prewar Japanese schools, but postwar educational reforms dropped it from curricula. Outside Japan, Western disaster science focused on technological solutions and seismology, overlooking indigenous and community-based warning systems as primitive or anecdotal rather than foundational models.
why_it_matters: His story directly inspired Japan's modern tsunami preparedness culture and the concept of 'tendenko'—individual evacuation without waiting for orders—which saved thousands during the 2011 Tōhoku tsunami. The United Nations adopted November 5 as World Tsunami Awareness Day in his honor in 2015, and his model of sacrificing personal wealth for communal resilience infrastructure remains a blueprint for disaster risk reduction programs worldwide.
